definition: To finance the build-out of AI data centres during the 2020s, an unprecedented amount of capital has been mobilised in the USA in particular amid a broad competition for global technnological supremacy in artificial intelligence.
details: Citigroup forecast that $2.8 trillion of capital expenditure would be required for AI data centre infrastructure by 2030, while McKinsey estimated that almost $7 trillion would be spent globally by that time. Between January and August 2024, Microsoft, Meta, Google and Amazon collectively spent $125 billion on AI data centres. According to S&P Global, $61 billion has been spent on the data centre market as a whole in 2025, while debt issuance for data centres was $182 billion during the same year. In 2026, major tech companies were estimated to spend $650 billion on AI data centres. Vendor financing has become a prominent feature of the build-out of artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure in the mid-2020s, as chipmakers and cloud-computing providers have extended capital, guarantees and purchase commitments to the companies that buy their hardware and services. The practice is most closely associated with Nvidia, whose graphics processing units (GPUs) power most large-scale AI training and inference, and with the "hyperscalers"—large cloud-computing operators such as Microsoft, Amazon and Google's parent Alphabet—and "frontier labs," a term used for AI developers building the most advanced large language models, principally OpenAI and Anthropic. Because these companies are simultaneously one another's investors, suppliers and customers, commentators have described the resulting arrangements as "circular financing" or "circular deals".

explainer.lead: AI build-out financing is the mix of cash, debt, investment, guarantees and long-term purchase commitments used to pay for AI data centres and computing infrastructure. Its scale matters because these commitments can shape technology supply, borrowing costs and financial risk well beyond the AI industry.

tiers.eli5: Building huge AI computer centres is a bit like building a chain of bakeries before you know how much bread people will buy. Sometimes the oven maker also lends you money or buys part of your business, and you promise to keep buying its ovens. This helps construction happen quickly, but everyone can lose money if bread sales disappoint.
tiers.practitioner: Teams securing AI compute may encounter financing tied to multi-year cloud leases, hardware purchases or capacity commitments rather than a simple pay-as-you-go purchase. Supplier equity, warrants and guarantees can help secure scarce chips and fund construction, but they also create counterparty concentration and commitments that may appear in financial-statement footnotes rather than as conventional debt.
tiers.paperLevel: AI build-out financing = operating cash flow + bond and other debt + equity investment + vendor capital, guarantees and purchase or lease commitments. In circular arrangements, supplier S provides capital to customer C while C commits to purchase S's hardware or services, so revenue, financing and equity exposure are linked. The arrangement can expand capacity when chips are scarce, but weak customer revenue can simultaneously reduce supplier sales and the value of the supplier's equity stake.

explainer.example: Nvidia held a 7% stake in CoreWeave and also agreed to buy $6.3 billion of its cloud services. CoreWeave rents access to computing based on Nvidia chips, illustrating how investment, chip supply and service purchases can reinforce one another.

usedIn.name: Microsoft–OpenAI infrastructure
usedIn.detail: Microsoft's investment in OpenAI has run alongside OpenAI's commitment to purchase $250 billion of Microsoft cloud services.

usedIn.name: Nvidia-backed neoclouds
usedIn.detail: Nvidia has invested in companies including CoreWeave, Nebius and Nscale that expand or rent access to AI computing infrastructure.

usedIn.name: Anthropic compute agreements
usedIn.detail: Anthropic's financing and compute arrangements have involved Amazon, Google, Nvidia, Microsoft and AMD.

usedIn.name: Data-centre bond markets
usedIn.detail: By 2026, the bond market had become the dominant source of financing for the AI build-out.

explainer.intuition: AI data centres require enormous spending before their operators necessarily earn matching revenue. Financing bridges that gap, and suppliers may help fund their own customers so that those customers can buy more chips, cloud capacity and infrastructure.
howItWorks: Hyperscalers, frontier labs and data-centre operators estimate the computing capacity they need and commit to building or leasing it.
They pay initially through operating cash flow, bonds, other debt, leases and outside investment.
A chipmaker or cloud provider may also invest in a customer, guarantee financing or make purchase commitments.
The customer uses that support to obtain infrastructure and commits to buying the supplier's chips or services.
If customer revenue falls short, purchasing can weaken while the supplier's equity investment loses value.
explainer.whyItMatters: These arrangements can unlock scarce computing capacity at exceptional speed, but overlapping investments and purchases concentrate financial exposure. Long-dated commitments and the growing use of debt can also affect companies and borrowers outside AI.
misconceptions: Circular financing is not simply one company buying another: the same firms can be investors, suppliers and customers at once.
A purchase or lease commitment is not necessarily recorded as traditional debt, even when it extends for decades.
Revenue generated through these arrangements can be real while still being difficult to separate from the investor's own capital deployment.

diagram.caption: Debt funds construction while supplier capital and customer purchases can form a circular flow.
